extracted.intended_audience: independent inventors, students, and researchers preparing prior-art searches before meeting a patent attorney or filing a patent
extracted.subtask_description: A practical, stepwise guide to conducting prior-art (patent) searches: brainstorming terms, using patent classification (CPC), using online patent-search tools (e.g., USPTO, Lens, Google Patents), reviewing retrieved patents, broadening searches, and deciding when a search is sufficiently exhaustive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brainstorm terms describing your invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Devise search keywords that focus on what the invention does rather than what it is called; patents often describe function instead of common names (e.g., US 3,541,541 titled 'X-Y POSITION INDICATOR FOR A DISPLAY SYSTEM' = computer mouse).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It's okay to try the common name (you may find some patents), but make a concerted effort to hone in on functional descriptions. Searching is iterative: inspect wording of any patents you find, watch for surprising alternative descriptions, and use discovered classification numbers to refine searches. Examples given include unusually worded historic patents (e.g., 'IMPROVEMENT IN TELEGRAPHY' = telephone).

rubrics_metrics.name: Start with broad keywords and narrow as needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin searches with significant, general terms (e.g., 'clock') and then narrow down if necessary once promising results or classification areas are identified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guide demonstrates starting broad (searching 'clock') to discover relevant CPC sections, then refining by drilling into relevant CPC classes (e.g., G04B) and subgroups (e.g., G04B 25/06 for cuckoo clocks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use patent classification (CPC) rather than keywords alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent Classification (particularly the Cooperative Patent Classification - CPC) is essential because keyword searching alone is often inadequate for patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The U.S. utility patent system has effectively adopted CPC; use CPC to locate groups of similar patents. The guide emphasizes moving from keywords to classification numbers and using those numbers to retrieve comprehensive sets of patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access and review the CPC schema on USPTO
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the USPTO 'Learn about patent classification' and the CPC Scheme pages to browse and understand CPC sections and their definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Browse by Section/Group to see the hierarchical CPC breakdown. Use the 'Find in Page' function to search for specific words within CPC pages. The guide walks through the steps and screenshots for locating CPC entries (e.g., G04B 25/06).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspect CPC classification definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: When you find a CPC code, read its definition(s) and linked broader/narrower groups to ensure it truly matches your invention domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some classification entries include brief descriptions and links to related groups (e.g., clicking the 'D' next to G04B 23/00 to see definitions). Definitions sometimes provide direct pointers to the most appropriate subgroup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be careful with query syntax when using search tools (e.g., lens.org)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different patent databases have quirks in query syntax; ensure you enter classification numbers in the format the tool expects (e.g., remove blanks between letter and numbers for lens.org: 'G04B25/06').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guide shows how to use Lens' 'Classifications' search and notes eliminating blank spaces and ignoring upper/lower case. Hovering UI elements (like a funnel icon) can let you 'Start new search' for a classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retrieve and review patents by CPC classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Once you have a promising CPC code, run a classification-based search to retrieve all patents assigned that code and review the returned list (titles, abstracts, claims).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the search results to expand view (abstracts and claims) and open full PDF documents for in-depth review. The guide demonstrates drilling down from CPC group to patent list and then viewing documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct in-depth review of selected patents using front-page information
rubrics_metrics.description: When you select promising patents, inspect front-page metadata (title, abstract, claims, inventor and assignee names) to judge relevance and to find new search leads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggestions: collect inventor/assignee names as search terms, note surprising terminology or classification numbers, and record how a patent differs from your idea (for later comparison). Use front-page info to decide which patents deserve deeper claim/description comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use inventor and assignee names as search avenues
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventor and assignee fields can reveal clusters of related patents and identify competitors/collaborators to follow in subsequent searches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep a list of names for follow-up searching. Searching by names may expose related patents not captured by your initial keywords or classifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize search results and take structured notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a personal database or reference manager (e.g., Zotero, Mendeley) to save patents of interest and record notes about relevance and differences to your idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tools to save PDFs and annotate why a particular patent does or does not preclude your idea. The guide suggests saving items to Zotero and taking notes for later in-depth comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow searches to be iterative and to generate new keywords/classifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat searching as a loop: reviewing retrieved patents will often produce new terminology and classification numbers that should be fed back into further searches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guide emphasizes that the inventor frequently must 'take over' the search as they learn domain-specific wording and classifications; repeatedly refine queries and classifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broaden searches across multiple databases and literature types
rubrics_metrics.description: To be thorough, search multiple patent databases (USPTO, EPO/espacenet, WIPO PATENTSCOPE, Google Patents), commercial indexes (Derwent Innovations Index), and academic literature databases (Scopus, Web of Science) that index patents and related literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guide lists specific resources and links (EPO/espacenet, PATENTSCOPE, Google Patents, Derwent, Scopus) and suggests also searching published literature beyond patent databases. Use international patent databases and design-specific registries as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search design patents separately from utility patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Design patents (registered designs) use different databases and classification approaches and should be searched separately from utility patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guide lists design-oriented resources (DesignView, ASEAN DesignView, Canadian Industrial Designs Database, Australian Industrial Design Database, German DPMAregister) and notes that the U.S. utility/design difference means the first patent in a list might be a design patent (less relevant to utility searches).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask stopping/coverage questions to decide when search is sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Use explicit self-check questions to decide if your search is thorough enough: did you try all reasonable databases, exhaust keywords and classifications, follow up on inventors/assignees, and are you still finding new relevant literature?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guide lists these exact questions as a final checklist: Have you thought of every reasonable database? Exhausted keywords/classifications? Followed up on inventors/assignees? Are you still discovering relevant patents or other literature you haven't seen before?

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of database-specific features (structure/expand/search facets)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different portals offer features such as 'Structure Search', 'Classifications' explorer, expand/view options, funnels/filters, and save/export functions that change how you locate and inspect patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Lens' 'Structure Search' and classification tree, UI funnel icon to start classification-based searches, 'Expand' view to show abstracts/claims, and save-to-Zotero buttons. Learn and exploit these features for efficient searching.
